newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Western economists welcome Ukraine revival plan.
newsitem.headline: Western economists welcome Ukraine revival plan.

text.p: Ukraine's new economic programme, geared at awakening a comatose industrial sector and attracting foreign investment, is a step in the right direction but may not go far enough, Western economists said on Wednesday.
"I am cheered by their efforts at deregulation and liberalisation of the economy," one U.S. economist told Reuters. "A common investor complaint is a lack of just these things."

The three-year plan, passed by parliament on Tuesday, promised to create 40 projects to attract investment for the country's largest exporters and pass 17 new laws to boost industry. It also said Ukraine would scrap many bureaucratic licensing requirements.
Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, seeking to attract foreign investment and to ease burdens on domestic producers, promised to reform the unwieldy tax system next year.
But one economist said the broad programme fell short by failing to secure land reform in this former bread basket.
Parliament had removed a clause that would have allowed the sale of land -- a contentious issue in Ukraine -- in an attempt to placate conservatives in parliament.
The economic programme, which Lazarenko said focused on boosting domestic production, also aims to retain value-added tax on many imports.
"No country has yet increased its economy without investment," said a European Union economist, who said the plan would have to go hand-in-hand with maintaining stability of the new hryvnia currency.
"You can't restructure without a strong currency, but you can't have a strong currency without restructuring."
Ukraine's central bank has ceased supporting the hryvnia on the currency exchange to allow the new monetary unit to find its own level.
Kiev officials have projected growth in industrial production of 1.7 percent next year, compared to a nine percent year-on-year drop in September.
"I think the economy will grow next year -- maybe not quickly, but it will happen," one economist said.
The 1997 draft budget also forecasts the first economic growth since the fall of Communism, with gross domestic product (GDP) seen rising 1.7 percent after a plunge of 11.8 percent last year.

But Lazarenko has made no promises to hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian workers who are owed $1.7 billion in wage arrears, except to say that the government will deal with the problem with monthly incremental payments.
Ukraine, which has been criticised in the past for the slow pace of privatisation, has attracted only about $1.5 billion in foreign investment since independence in 1991.
It is now trying to speed up privatisation.
One investment fund manager said that faster privatisation could cover a large part of the wage bill.
But he warned that the former Soviet republic's last chance to prove itself could be in 1997, before parliamentary elections in 1998 and presidential elections set for 1999.
Such political events could cause investors to wait even longer before investing, he said.
"The window of opportunity is very short," he said. "If Ukraine loses this opportunity we'll be waiting until the year 2000."
